'''Marcetta York Darensbourg''' is an American inorganic chemist. She is a Distinguished Professor of Chemistry at [[Texas A&M University]]. Her research focuses on bioinorganic and organometallic chemistry, particularly synthetic models of [[hydrogenase]] enzymes and [[metal nitrosyl complex|iron nitrosyl complexes]]. She is known for her work on metallodithiolate ligands and biomimetic catalysts relevant to hydrogen metabolism. In 2017, she was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].

== Early life ==
'''Marcetta Bernice (York) Darensbourg''' was born May 4, 1942, in [[Artemus, Kentucky]]. She is the daughter of school teachers Atlas H. York and Elsie Walton York. She has an older sister, Mary Lucille York, and a younger brother, Larry Hercules York. Darensbourg attended Knox Central High School in [[Barbourville, Kentucky]].<ref name="TAMUDarensbourg" /> During high school, she developed an interest in science, influenced in part by a teacher, Mrs. Bolton, who taught biology, physics, and chemistry.<ref name="TAMUDarensbourg">{{cite web | url = http://www.chem.tamu.edu/rgroup/marcetta/myd.html | title = Marcetta Y. Darensbourg | publisher = [[Texas A&M University]]}}</ref>

== Education ==
Darensbourg received a B.S. in chemistry from [[Union College (Kentucky)|Union College]] in 1963 and a Ph.D. in inorganic chemistry from the [[University of Illinois]] under the supervision of [[Theodore L. Brown]] in 1967.<ref name="TAMUDarensbourg" /> Her doctoral work focused on kinetic studies of organolithium reactions.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Kinetic studies of some organolithium reactions.|date=1967|language=English|first=Marcetta Bernice|last=York|oclc = 498417447}}</ref>

== Career ==
Darensbourg was an assistant professor at [[Vassar College]] from 1967 to 1969. From 1971 to 1982, she taught at [[Tulane University]], where she attained the rank of professor. In 1982, she joined [[Texas A&M University]] as a professor, together with [[Donald J. Darensbourg]], and was named Distinguished Professor in 2010.<ref name=distinguished>{{cite press release | url = http://www.science.tamu.edu/articles/756 | publisher = [[Texas A&M University]] | title = Five Science Faculty Honored as Distinguished Professors | date = 6 Sep 2010 | access-date = 18 July 2011 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110928162436/http://www.science.tamu.edu/articles/756 | archive-date = 28 September 2011 | url-status = dead }}</ref> Her research includes studies of hydrogenase enzymes and related metal complexes.

Darensbourg has served on the board of ''[[Inorganic Syntheses]]'' and was editor of volume 32.<ref name="InorgSynth32">{{cite book |title=Inorganic Syntheses, Volume 32 |editor=Marcetta Y. Darensbourg |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=1998 |isbn=9780471249214 |doi=10.1002/9780470132630}}</ref> In 2011, she was elected a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{cite press release | title = Darensbourg Elected Fellow of American Academy of Arts and Sciences | url = http://www.science.tamu.edu/articles/793 | date = 19 Apr 2011 | publisher = [[Texas A&M University]]}}</ref>

In 2017, she was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="NASDarensbourg">{{cite web |title=Marcetta Y. Darensbourg |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/marcetta-y-darensbourg-wjprh0/ |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=March 22, 2026}}</ref>

== Research ==

=== Organolithium chemistry ===
Darensbourg studied the kinetics and aggregation behavior of [[organolithium]] compounds, including tert-butyllithium, using spectroscopic methods such as <sup>7</sup>Li NMR. Her work examined factors influencing dissociation and exchange processes in these systems.<ref name="Kimura1970">{{cite journal|last1=Darensbourg|first1=Marcetta Y.|last2=Kimura|first2=Bert Y.|last3=Hartwell|first3=George E.|last4=Brown|first4=Theodore Lawrence|title=Organometallic exchange reactions. X. Cross-association of tert-butyllithium. Kinetics of tert-butyllithium dissociation|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=1970-03-01|volume=92|issue=5|pages=1236–1242|doi=10.1021/ja00708a022}}</ref>

=== Metal carbonyl chemistry ===
Darensbourg has studied the reactivity of [[metal carbonyl complex|metal carbonyl]] complexes, particularly the factors governing nucleophilic attack and ligand behavior in [[transition metal]] systems. Spectroscopic studies of carbene pentacarbonyl complexes demonstrated that carbene ligands can act as strong sigma donors and pi acceptors relative to carbonyl ligands.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Darensbourg|first1=Marcetta Y.|last2=Darensbourg|first2=Donald J.|title=Spectroscopic Studies of Some Carbene Pentacarbonyl Complexes of Chromium(0) and Tungsten(0).|journal=Inorganic Chemistry|date=1970|volume=9|issue=1|pages=32–39|doi=10.1021/ic50083a007}}</ref> Additional studies examined how ligand environments influence the site and selectivity of nucleophilic attack in metal carbonyl systems.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Darensbourg|first1=Donald J.|last2=Darensbourg|first2=Marcetta Y.|title=Reactions of Transition Metal Carbonyls with Organolithium Compounds. II. Prediction of Nucleophilic Attack at Carbon and Resultant Stereochemistry.|journal=Inorganic Chemistry|date=1970|volume=9|issue=7|pages=1691–694|doi=10.1021/ic50089a016}}</ref>

=== Hydrogenase mimics ===
Darensbourg has developed synthetic models of [[hydrogenase]] enzyme active sites, particularly iron- and nickel-based organometallic complexes that mimic biological hydrogen metabolism. These systems can carry out catalytic hydrogen production in the absence of the native protein environment.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lyon|first1=Erica J|last2=Zhao|first2=Xuan|last3=Georgakaki|first3=Irene P.|last4=Darensbourg|first4=Marcetta Y.|title=The Organometallic Active Site of [Fe]hydrogenase: Models and Entatic States|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|date=2003|volume=100|issue=7|pages=3683–3688|bibcode=2003PNAS..100.3683D|doi=10.1073/pnas.0536955100|pmc=152982|pmid=12642671|doi-access=free}}</ref> Her work has also examined factors affecting catalytic performance, including oxygen sensitivity and mechanisms of inactivation.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tye|first1=Jesse W.|last2=Hall|first2=Michael B.|last3=Darensbourg|first3=Marcetta Y.|title=Better than Platinum? Fuel Cells Energized by Enzymes.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|date=2005|volume=102|issue=47|pages=16911–16912|bibcode=2005PNAS..10216911T|doi=10.1073/pnas.0508740102|pmc=1288019|pmid=16286638|doi-access=free}}</ref> More recent studies have explored structural variations in hydrogenase-inspired complexes, including chalcogenide-containing systems, to improve catalytic activity and tolerance to oxygen.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Xuemei |last2=Darensbourg |first2=Marcetta Y. |date=2020 |title=The roles of chalcogenides in O 2 protection of H 2 ase active sites |journal=Chemical Science |language=en |volume=11 |issue=35 |pages=9366–9377 |doi=10.1039/D0SC02584D |issn=2041-6520 |pmc=8161538 |pmid=34094202}}</ref>

=== Metallodithiolates chemistry ===
[[File:Wiki_Figure-2.jpg|thumb|Examples of nickel and palladium dithiolate ligands]]
Darensbourg has studied metallodithiolate ligands as building blocks for transition metal complexes relevant to bioinorganic chemistry. Her work has examined how these ligands coordinate metals such as nickel, iron, and cobalt, influencing electronic structure and reactivity in catalytic systems.<ref>{{Cite == Awards ==
Darensbourg has received several honors for her contributions to chemistry and education, including the [[American Chemical Society]] Willard Gibbs Award (2019),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Willard Gibbs Award |url=https://chicagoacs.org/Willard_Gibbs_Award |access-date=2026-05-20 |website=chicagoacs.org}}</ref> the American Chemical Society Award in Organometallic Chemistry (2017),<ref>{{Cite web |title=2017 Recipients |url=https://www.acs.org/funding/awards/national/recipients/2017-recipients.html |access-date=2024-04-12 |website=American Chemical Society |language=en}}</ref> and the [[Southeastern Conference|SEC]] Professor of the Year award (2018).<ref>{{Cite web |title=SEC Faculty Achievement Awards {{!}} SEC Academics {{!}} SEC |url=https://www.thesecu.com/programs/sec-faculty-achievement-awards/ |access-date=2024-04-12 |website=SECU |language=en-US}}</ref> She has also received teaching and mentoring awards from [[Texas A&M University]] and [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]] (2016),<ref>{{Cite web |title=College of Science Honors 2016 Award Winners – TAMU Physics & Astronomy |url=https://physics.tamu.edu/college-of-science-honors-2016-award-winners/ |access-date=2024-04-12 |website=physics.tamu.edu}}</ref> the Kosolapoff Award from [[Auburn University]] (2018),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kosolapoff Award - Chemistry & Biochemistry - AU COSAM |url=https://www.auburn.edu/cosam/departments/chemistry/colloquium/kosolapoff_old.htm |access-date=2024-10-16 | website=www.auburn.edu}}</ref>,  and the Eminent Scholar Award from the Texas A&M Aggie Women Network (2024).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Henton |first=Lesley |date=2024-10-15 |title=Chemist Marcetta Darensbourg Honored With Eminent Scholar Award |url=https://today.tamu.edu/2024/10/15/chemist-marcetta-darensbourg-honored-with-eminent-scholar-award/ |access-date=2024-10-16 |website=Texas A&M Today |language=en-US}}</ref>
